analysis.one_liner: Bans coal companies from promising, instead of paying, to cover their own mine cleanup costs.
analysis.headline: The bill won 13 cosponsors and a single subcommittee hearing in September 2019, then never received a committee or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Coal companies are supposed to post a bond — money guaranteed up front — so that if they walk away from a mine, someone else's money is available to restore the land. The bill would have banned "self-bonding," where a company simply promises in writing to pay cleanup costs later with no cash or guarantee behind it, and would have forced existing self-bonds to be replaced with real surety or collateral bonds. It also set rules to make sure bond collateral was worth something and let regulators count executive pay as backing.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would no longer be exposed to paying for cleaning up strip mines if a coal company goes bankrupt, because the bill bans self-bonding (a company's own written promise to pay, with no money set aside) and requires real surety or collateral bonds [S2, S3]. People living near coal mines also benefit, since a funded bond makes it more likely abandoned sites actually get reclaimed rather than left as unfunded liabilities [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bars the federal mining office and state regulators from accepting any new self-bonds for coal mine reclamation, so cleanup money must be guaranteed up front by a third party or posted as collateral [S2, S3].

Requires existing self-bonds and corporate surety bonds to be converted to real surety or collateral bonds, closing the gap where a company's paper promise is all that stands between taxpayers and a cleanup bill [S2, S3].

Stops companies from posting worthless collateral by forbidding bonds backed by the coal itself, the mine, land above the mine, or equipment unlikely to keep resale value, and requires collateral to be re-valued every three years [S3].

Lets regulators count executives' salaries and bonuses, including at affiliated companies, as bond collateral, so a failing company cannot shield the money that would actually be available for cleanup [S3].

Directs the Interior Department to write rules limiting how many coal reclamation bonds any single surety company can issue and how much cash it must hold, reducing the risk that the insurer backing the bond fails too [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mining companies, which would have to replace promises-to-pay with real surety or collateral bonds worth the full estimated cleanup cost, including posting collateral that cannot be coal assets or equipment with little resale value [S3]. Mine owners with weak finances would find bonding harder or more expensive, and surety companies would face new federal rules limiting how many coal reclamation bonds they could issue and how much collateral they must hold [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal companies and surety bond insurers

drawbacks.text: Requiring full surety or collateral bonds ties up significant capital at every affected mine, and the added cost would fall hardest on financially weaker mining companies — precisely the ones most likely to leave taxpayers with an unfunded cleanup [S3].

The industry's standard objection is that self-bonding lets strong companies avoid diverting capital into bonds they may never need; forcing conversion of existing self-bonds could raise mining costs and add pressure on already-struggling coal firms and the communities that depend on them.
Concentrating cleanup risk in surety companies creates its own failure risk, which the bill only partially addresses through new collateral and concentration rules for corporate sureties [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: taxpayers and coal communities stop carrying the risk that a bankrupt coal company leaves its mess behind, and coal companies bear the cost of posting real financial guarantees instead of paper promises. The main cost is higher bonding expenses in an already strained industry, which could accelerate closures in mining towns — but those closures are exactly the scenario where self-bonding leaves cleanup bills unpaid. The bill was narrowly focused and did not address the large backlog of abandoned mines already unfunded, so its benefit, while real, was limited in scope.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee after a single subcommittee hearing in its first week and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 20, 2019 and referred the same day to the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee [S5].
The subcommittee held a hearing on September 24, 2019 — the only recorded action beyond referral [S5].
The committee never reported the bill out and the House never voted on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal companies that wanted to keep self-bonding are better off, since the option to promise rather than pay for cleanup survived. Taxpayers and communities near mines remain exposed to the risk of unfunded reclamation costs if a mining company fails.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal companies that kept self-bonding flexibility

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all 14 recorded supporters — the sponsor and 13 cosponsors — were House Democrats, and the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would take away self-bonding, which lets companies promise to pay cleanup costs without setting aside money, and force existing self-bonds to be replaced with real financial guarantees. The industry's saving on cleanup is money that falls on taxpayers when a company fails.

Requiring surety and collateral bonds instead of self-bonds would create demand for surety insurance. New federal limits on how much coal-reclamation business any one surety could carry, and minimum collateral rules, would also constrain how the industry operates.
The bill directly reduces the chance that federal or state governments absorb reclamation costs when a mining company cannot pay, the exact risk self-bonding creates.
